flatcap-1: Layout ①: your version — a magnet under the centre, “south pole” on the underside. Honestly computed: a vertical dipole really does give a dip-zero circle (at r = √2 × its depth — the depth is chosen to put that circle on the real magnetic equator, red dashed). But past it the field dies as 1/r³ and the dip goes shallow, not steep: nowhere on the disc can it pass −35°, yet Dunedin measures −72°. The horizontal pull fades to ~4 μT at the wall — a fifth of what a Melbourne compass measurably feels.
flatcap-2: Layout ②: the other arrangement flat-Earth writers actually propose — a pole at the centre, its opposite spread along the rim (“the ice wall is the south pole”). The ring is exactly as strong as the centre pole, as the two poles of any magnet are; its burial depth is fitted to the ten measured dips. The arrows give the direction of the field: each line leaves the rim ring, arcs over, enters the centre pole and runs back to the rim inside the buried magnetised disc (black line), so every line is a closed loop and none ends. No depth can put its dip-zero circle on the real equator (red dashed): it falls ~3,600 km farther out, so Singapore and São Paulo read a downward dip where needles point up. Past it the south stays shallow — Melbourne −9°, Dunedin −12°, against measured −69° and −72° — no point on the disc passes −69°, and the centre pole makes the Arctic read ~190 μT, over three times what is measured.
note-tpl: At λ = {lat}° the map distance from the pole is {r}k km. The globe and flat ① agree by construction on the 10,000 km circle — that is where ① spent its free parameter; flat ② cannot put its level circle there, and no burial depth brings it closer than 13,200 km. Move the slider off it and watch them separate: the globe's H stays strong enough to steer a compass everywhere except the two dip poles themselves; flat ① can never dip past −35° and its field dies as 1/r³; flat ② points down where the globe points up, between 10,000 and 13,600 km, then stays shallow across the whole south and never passes −69°.
citynote: λ is dipole-frame magnetic latitude (approx.); measured values are IGRF-era, rounded. * São Paulo and Cape Town sit in the South Atlantic weak patch — the largest non-dipole anomaly on Earth — which is why their measured |B| runs ~30% under the dipole column while the dip keeps its southern sign. The dipole column lands within ~10° and ~±30% everywhere, with the right sign pattern; the flat columns miss the southern dips by up to 65° and the strength by a factor of 3 to 10, always in the same tell-tale way: too strong in the Arctic, too weak and too level in the far south.

At your λ = {lat}°  (r = {r}k km on the map):
globe → I = {gI}°, |B| = {gB} μT, H = {gH} μT
flat ① → I = {f1I}°, |B| = {f1B} μT, H = {f1H} μT
flat ② → I = {f2I}°, |B| = {f2B} μT, H = {f2H} μT
exp5v-tpl: Verdict rule: if readings across latitudes follow either amber column — southern dip frozen above −35° with fields collapsing several-fold (①), or a level circle ~3,600 km south of the observed magnetic equator, a south that never dips past −69° and Arctic fields near 200 μT (②) — the flat disc is vindicated and the dipole-sphere refuted. If instead I flips sign at one circle, follows tan I = 2 tan λ to within the stated ~10°, and |B| stays within ~22–67 μT with a single I = −90° point in Antarctica, the sphere stands. At your latitude the two shapes disagree by {diff}° of dip — far beyond any instrument error.

f3d-cap: The field lines of the three models in 3D — drag to turn them, or use the arrow keys. They are computed from the same fields as the rest of this tab, each panel at true scale (bar at the bottom left; the three panels have different scales). The arrows give the direction of the field. On the globe the lines leave the southern hemisphere, enter the northern one and close through the Earth (the liquid core in orange). Under flat disc ① they close through the buried magnet. Under flat disc ② they leave the rim ring, above or below the plane of the poles, enter the centre pole and run back to the rim inside the buried magnetised disc (grey, black lines). In all three, every line is a closed loop: none begins or ends. Pale lines run below the surface or inside the Earth.
